title: Book Eight (1811 - 12) — Chapter 13
paragraphs: Count Rostov took the girls to Countess Bezukhova's. A good many people were there, but nearly all of them were strangers to Natasha. The count was annoyed to find that the company was made up almost entirely of men and women known for the looseness of their behavior. Mademoiselle George stood in a corner of the drawing room, surrounded by young men. Several Frenchmen were present, among them Metivier, who had been a regular in Helene's house ever since she arrived in Moscow. The count decided not to sit down to cards, not to let his girls out of his sight, and to leave as soon as Mademoiselle George had finished her performance.

Anatole was standing at the door, plainly watching for the Rostovs. As soon as he had greeted the count, he went over to Natasha and followed her. The moment she saw him, she was seized by the same feeling she'd had at the opera — vanity flattered by his admiration, and fear that there was no moral barrier between them.

Helene welcomed Natasha with delight and went on loudly about her beauty and her dress. Soon after they arrived, Mademoiselle George left the room to change her costume. In the drawing room people began arranging chairs and taking their seats. Anatole moved a chair for Natasha and was about to sit down next to her, but the count, who never let her out of his sight, took the seat himself. Anatole sat down behind her.
Mademoiselle George, her arms bare, fat and dimpled, a red shawl draped over one shoulder, stepped into the space left clear for her and struck an unnatural pose. Excited whispering could be heard.

Mademoiselle George looked sternly and gloomily at the audience and began to recite some French verses about her guilty love for her son. In places she raised her voice, in others she dropped to a whisper and lifted her head in triumph; sometimes she stopped and made hoarse sounds, rolling her eyes.
"Adorable! Divine! Delicious!" came from every side.

Natasha looked at the fat actress, but she neither saw nor heard nor understood anything of what was going on in front of her. She only felt herself carried away once more into this strange, senseless world — so far from her old one — a world where it was impossible to tell what was good or bad, sensible or senseless. Anatole sat behind her, and aware of how close he was, she felt a frightened sense of expectancy.
After the first monologue the whole company stood up and crowded around Mademoiselle George, showing their enthusiasm.
"How beautiful she is!" Natasha said to her father, who had also risen and was making his way through the crowd toward the actress.
"I don't think so, when I look at you!" said Anatole, following Natasha. He said it at a moment when only she could hear him. "You are enchanting... from the moment I saw you I have never ceased..."

"Come, come, Natasha!" said the count, turning back to fetch his daughter. "How beautiful she is!" Natasha said nothing; she stepped up to her father and looked at him with surprised, questioning eyes.
After a few more recitations Mademoiselle George left, and Countess Bezukhova invited her guests into the ballroom.

The count wanted to go home, but Helene begged him not to spoil her impromptu ball, and the Rostovs stayed. Anatole asked Natasha for a waltz, and as they danced he pressed her waist and her hand and told her she was bewitching and that he loved her. During the écossaise, which she also danced with him, Anatole said nothing whenever they happened to be alone, but only gazed at her. Natasha raised frightened eyes to him, but his look and smile were so full of confident tenderness that, while looking at him, she could not say what she had to say. She lowered her eyes.
"Don't say such things to me. I am engaged and I love another," she said quickly.... She glanced at him.
Anatole was neither upset nor hurt by what she had said.
"Don't speak to me of that! What can I do?" said he. "I tell you I am madly, madly in love with you! Is it my fault that you are enchanting?... It's our turn to begin."

Natasha, animated and excited, looked around her with wide, frightened eyes and seemed merrier than usual. She understood hardly anything that happened that evening. They danced the écossaise and the Grossvater. Her father asked her to come home, but she begged to stay. Wherever she went and whoever she was talking to, she felt his eyes on her. Later she remembered asking her father to let her go to the dressing room to fix her dress, and Helene following her and laughingly speaking of her brother's love, and then meeting Anatole again in the little sitting room. Helene had vanished, leaving them alone, and Anatole had taken her hand and said in a tender voice:
"I can't visit you, but is it possible that I shall never see you? I love you madly. Can I never...?" and, blocking her way, he brought his face close to hers.
His large, glittering, masculine eyes were so near hers that she saw nothing but them.
"Natalie?" he whispered questioningly, while she felt her hands being painfully squeezed. "Natalie?"
"I don't understand. I have nothing to say," her eyes replied.

Burning lips pressed against hers, and at that same instant she felt herself released, and Helene's footsteps and the rustle of her dress were heard in the room. Natasha looked around at her, and then, red and trembling, threw Anatole a frightened, questioning look and moved toward the door.
"One word, just one, for God's sake!" cried Anatole.
She stopped. She wanted so badly to hear a word from him that would explain what had happened — something she could find no answer to.
"Natalie, just a word, only one!" he kept saying, plainly not knowing what to say, and he went on repeating it until Helene came up to them.
Helene went back to the drawing room with Natasha. The Rostovs left without staying for supper.

When she got home, Natasha did not sleep all night. She was tormented by a question she could not solve: did she love Anatole or Prince Andrew? She loved Prince Andrew — she remembered clearly how deeply she loved him. But she loved Anatole too, there was no doubt of that. "Otherwise how could all this have happened?" she thought. "If I could smile back at him when I said good-by after that, if I let it come to this, it means I loved him from the first. It means he is kind, noble, and splendid, and I couldn't help loving him. What am I to do if I love him and the other one too?" she asked herself, unable to find any answer to these terrible questions.
